description: Food security, selective breeding, genetic modification, tissue culture and biological control.
content_html:
The Challenge of Food Security

Food security means ensuring that all people have reliable access to sufficient, nutritious food. With the global population growing rapidly, achieving food security is one of the most pressing challenges biologists and agricultural scientists face. Key threats include: population growth (more people need more food), climate change (droughts, floods and extreme weather damage crops), rising costs (fuel and fertiliser price increases raise food prices), conflict (war disrupts farming and distribution) and water scarcity (unreliable irrigation).

Key Fact

Food security is threatened by population growth, climate change, rising costs, conflict and water scarcity. Biologists develop scientific solutions to increase food production sustainably.

Selective Breeding

Selective breeding (also called artificial selection) is when humans choose organisms with the most desirable characteristics and breed them together over many generations. Over time, the frequency of the desired alleles increases in the population. Examples include:

• Breeding cattle that produce greater quantities of milk or have faster growth rates.
• Developing wheat varieties resistant to fungal diseases such as wheat rust.
• Selecting dogs with specific temperaments and physical traits for different working roles.
• Breeding crop plants with increased yield per hectare.

Selective breeding is effective but has a key limitation: it reduces genetic diversity within the population. Repeated breeding from a small gene pool makes populations more uniform. This means a new pathogen or environmental change to which they have no resistance could devastate the entire population. Selective breeding can also cause health issues in animals when extreme traits are selected (e.g. breathing difficulties in flat-faced dog breeds).

Genetic modification (GM) involves inserting a gene from one organism directly into the DNA of another to give it a new characteristic. Unlike selective breeding, GM can introduce entirely new characteristics from a different species in a single generation. The process involves: identifying the desired gene in a donor organism; cutting it out using restriction enzymes; inserting it into the target organism’s DNA using a vector (often a bacterium or a virus).

GM crops have been engineered to be resistant to insect pests (reducing the need for insecticides), resistant to herbicides (allowing weeds to be killed without harming the crop), tolerant to drought conditions, or capable of producing greater yields. One widely discussed example is golden rice, which has been modified to produce beta-carotene (a precursor to vitamin A) — potentially addressing vitamin A deficiency in populations where rice is a staple food.

Concerns about GM crops include: the possibility that GM genes could spread to wild plant relatives through cross-pollination, creating herbicide-resistant ‘superweeds’; potential unknown long-term effects on human health or ecosystems; ethical objections to interfering with natural genetic sequences; and the concentration of seed ownership in the hands of large corporations, which may disadvantage smallholder farmers.

Key Fact

GM crops can be pest-resistant, drought-tolerant or more nutritious. Concerns include gene transfer to wild plants, unknown long-term effects and ethical objections. Selective breeding reduces genetic diversity over time; GM can introduce new traits in one generation.

Tissue Culture

Tissue culture is a technique used to propagate plants rapidly by taking small samples of plant tissue (called explants), sterilising them and growing them on a nutrient medium containing the correct balance of plant growth hormones. Each explant develops into a complete, whole plant that is genetically identical to the parent plant. This allows large numbers of plants to be produced quickly and reliably from a single parent — useful for preserving rare or endangered plant species, for multiplying commercially high-value varieties such as orchids, and for producing disease-free planting stock. Because all the plants produced are clones, they share the same genetic advantages as the selected parent — but also the same vulnerabilities. If a disease emerges that one plant cannot resist, none of the clones will be resistant either.

Biological control uses living organisms instead of chemical pesticides to manage pests. Examples include introducing ladybirds to feed on aphid colonies on crop plants, or using parasitic wasps that lay eggs inside caterpillars, whose larvae then kill the host. Biological control avoids chemical pollution and is self-sustaining once established, but it can be unpredictable — the introduced organism may become invasive itself, attack non-target species or fail to control the pest effectively.

Integrated pest management (IPM) combines chemical and biological approaches, using pesticides only when pest numbers exceed a threshold and relying on natural predators where possible. This minimises chemical use and environmental impact while protecting crop yields.

Sustainable farming practices that help with food security include crop rotation (alternating crops each season to prevent soil mineral depletion and reduce pest build-up), organic farming (using natural fertilisers and biological control instead of synthetic chemicals) and hydroponics (growing plants in nutrient solutions without soil, allowing year-round production in controlled environments with less water use than traditional farming).

Key Fact

Tissue culture produces many identical plants from a single parent rapidly. Biological control uses natural predators rather than chemicals. Crop rotation and hydroponics are examples of sustainable farming practices that increase food security.
exam_tip_html: For questions comparing selective breeding and genetic modification, be precise: selective breeding uses natural reproduction over many generations and cannot introduce entirely new genes; GM directly inserts a gene from another species and can produce the change in one generation. For evaluate questions on GM crops, ensure you cover both sides — advantages (higher yield, pest resistance) and concerns (gene spread, ethical issues) — and reach a conclusion. For ‘3 marks — Explain’ questions on food security threats, name the specific threat, explain the mechanism (how it reduces food supply), and link it to a consequence for people.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Food security is threatened by population growth, climate change, rising costs, conflict and water scarcity. Selective breeding develops improved crop and livestock varieties over many generations but reduces genetic diversity.
  • Genetic modification inserts a gene from one organism into another to give it a new characteristic in one generation. GM crops can be pest-resistant, drought-tolerant or more nutritious, but concerns include gene transfer to wild plants and unknown long-term effects.
  • Tissue culture rapidly propagates genetically identical plants. Biological control and integrated pest management reduce reliance on chemical pesticides. Crop rotation, organic farming and hydroponics are sustainable practices that support long-term food security.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the process of genetic modification?
A) Breeding organisms with desirable traits over many generations
B) Inserting a gene from one organism into the DNA of another organism
C) Growing plant cells in nutrient solution to produce identical clones
D) Using natural predators to control pest populations
practice_questions.marks: B) Inserting a gene from one organism into the DNA of another organism [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two threats to food security caused by climate change.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: droughts reduce crop yields [accept reduced rainfall]; floods destroy crops and farmland; extreme weather events damage harvests; changes in growing seasons [1 mark for two correct threats]

practice_questions.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of using biological control to manage crop pests.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantage: does not use chemical pesticides / no chemical pollution / self-sustaining once established [1 mark]
Disadvantage: introduced organism may become invasive / may attack non-target species / can be unpredictable / may not control the pest effectively [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how selective breeding increases food production and state one risk associated with the process.
practice_questions.marks: Humans select organisms with desirable characteristics (e.g. high yield, disease resistance) and breed them together [1 mark]; over many generations, the frequency of desirable alleles increases in the population, producing consistently improved varieties [1 mark]; risk: reduces genetic diversity so the population may be vulnerable to new diseases or environmental changes [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A farmer is considering using genetically modified herbicide-resistant crops instead of conventional varieties.
Explain what is meant by genetic modification and evaluate whether the farmer should use GM crops.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate explanation of GM process; balanced evaluation with developed arguments for and against; justified conclusion.
Secure: Correct explanation; arguments on both sides with some development; conclusion present.
Developing: Partial explanation; limited evaluation; one-sided response.
Emerging: Vague description; few relevant points.

Explanation points: a gene conferring herbicide resistance is identified in another organism; cut out using restriction enzymes and inserted into crop plant DNA using a vector; all offspring carry the new gene.
For: herbicide-resistant crops allow blanket herbicide application to kill weeds without harming the crop, reducing competition and increasing yield; reduces the number of herbicide applications needed.
Against: herbicide-resistance gene could spread to wild plant relatives via cross-pollination, creating herbicide-resistant weeds that are difficult to control; concern about unknown long-term effects on ecosystems; ethical objections; seed ownership concerns.
Conclusion should weigh advantages against specific concerns in the farming context.

practice_questions.text: Describe how tissue culture is used to produce large numbers of crop plants and explain one advantage of this method.
practice_questions.marks:
Small samples of tissue (explants) are taken from the parent plant and grown on a sterile nutrient medium, producing many genetically identical plants rapidly [1 mark]
Advantage: any one from — produces large numbers quickly; all plants have the same desirable characteristics as the parent; can be done year-round; produces disease-free stock; useful for preserving rare varieties [1 mark]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the main disadvantage of selective breeding over many generations?
options: It takes only one generation to work
It reduces genetic diversity, increasing vulnerability to disease
It can introduce genes from different species

knowledge_checks.q: Which technique rapidly produces many genetically identical plants from a single parent by growing tissue on a nutrient medium?
Biological control uses _____ organisms instead of chemical pesticides to manage pest populations.
Genetic modification can introduce a completely new characteristic in a single generation, unlike _____ which requires many generations.
Match each agricultural technique to what it does:
right: Breeding organisms with desired traits over many generations
Inserting a gene from another species into an organism's DNA
Growing plant tissue on nutrient medium to produce identical clones
Using natural predators to reduce pest populations

flashcard_questions.a: Reliable access to enough affordable, nutritious food for the whole population.
Deliberately breeding organisms with desirable traits over many generations to improve a population.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main genetic risk of selective breeding?
flashcard_questions.a: Reduced genetic diversity, making the population vulnerable to new diseases or environmental change.

flashcard_questions.q: How does genetic modification differ from selective breeding?
flashcard_questions.a: GM inserts a gene from another species directly in one generation; selective breeding uses natural reproduction over many generations.

flashcard_questions.q: What is golden rice modified to produce?
Name one concern about GM crops and gene spread.
flashcard_questions.a: GM genes could spread to wild plant relatives via cross-pollination, creating herbicide-resistant weeds.
Growing plant tissue on a sterile nutrient medium to produce many genetically identical plants rapidly.
Using living organisms (e.g. natural predators) to reduce pest populations instead of chemical pesticides.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of biological control.
flashcard_questions.a: Advantage: no chemical pollution. Disadvantage: the introduced organism may become invasive.

flashcard_questions.q: How does crop rotation help maintain food security?
flashcard_questions.a: Alternating crops each season prevents soil mineral depletion and reduces pest build-up.

glossary_terms.definition: Having reliable access to enough affordable, nutritious food to meet the dietary needs of the population.
The deliberate breeding of organisms with desirable characteristics over many generations by humans, to produce offspring with improved traits.
The direct alteration of an organism's DNA by inserting a gene from another species to give it a new desirable characteristic.
A technique for growing plant cells or small tissue fragments on a nutrient medium under sterile conditions to produce many genetically identical plants from a single parent.
Using living organisms to reduce the population of a pest species, such as introducing a natural predator to control crop-damaging insects.
A pest control strategy that combines chemical and biological methods, using pesticides only when necessary and relying on natural predators where possible to minimise environmental impact.
